analysis.one_liner: Lets states set up publicly run universal health plans, funded with redirected Medicare and Medicaid money plus a new income tax surtax.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees in June 1991, it died there when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill let any state elect to set up a universal, comprehensive health insurance plan run by a public, nonprofit authority on its behalf. In exchange, the federal government would redirect that state's Medicare and Medicaid payments to the state and add a block grant to cover the uninsured, the underinsured, long-term care, and out-of-pocket costs. The new money would be raised through a surtax on federal income taxes, held in a dedicated trust fund. Participating states would have to cover everyone on uniform terms, ban extra billing by doctors and hospitals, and put hospitals on fixed annual budgets.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of states that join — including the roughly 37 million uninsured and 50 million underinsured Americans the bill cites — would get hospital, physician, and surgical-dental care with no extra billing and no financial barriers, plus long-term and home care coverage. Medicare beneficiaries in participating states would have their Part B premiums paid by the state.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of participating states, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Every resident of a participating state would be entitled to hospital, physician, and surgical-dental services on uniform terms, regardless of income, with no minimum residence or waiting period beyond three months.
The bill would ban extra billing: doctors, dentists, and hospitals could not charge patients beyond what the state plan pays, and access could not be impeded by charges to patients.

States would receive their Medicare and Medicaid dollars as direct payments plus a block grant equal to 6 percent of the state's total health spending, to insure the uninsured and underinsured, extend long-term and home care, and cover costs currently paid out of pocket.

Plans must be run on a nonprofit basis by a public authority accountable to the state government, and the state plan would override federal ERISA rules that otherwise shield employer insurance from state regulation.

States could use plan funds to recruit doctors to underserved areas through scholarships and student debt retirement, and could negotiate compensation with physician and dentist organizations without violating antitrust law.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a surtax added on top of regular income tax and the alternative minimum tax, sized each year to replace the revenue spent on the block grants. In participating states, insurance companies would lose their role in covered care, and doctors and hospitals would face fixed global budgets and an end to balance billing patients.
analysis.who_pays_short: Income taxpayers and, in participating states, insurers and providers

drawbacks.text: The bill pays for the new block grant with a surtax on every taxpayer's income tax and minimum tax liability, so federal tax bills would rise even for people in states that never join.

Participation is entirely voluntary: a state only gets the federal money if it elects to participate and its plan is certified, so there is no guarantee any state would actually establish universal coverage.

Hospitals and nursing facilities would be paid through binding global budgets, and practitioners would have to accept the plan's payment as compensation in full — a real constraint on provider revenue that critics could argue risks access or quality, which the bill addresses only with utilization review and an inspector general.
Participating states and their public authorities would be exempt from federal antitrust laws, a broad immunity that would be hard to oversee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is honest and stated up front: taxpayers pay a visibly higher income tax surtax, and in return residents of participating states get first-dollar coverage with no extra billing and no premiums for Medicare Part B. Because Medicare and Medicaid money is redirected rather than duplicated, and the surtax is set each year to exactly replace block-grant spending, the design is budget-neutral rather than deficit-financed. The main design weaknesses are that participation is voluntary (so national coverage depends on state-by-state choices) and that global budgets and an antitrust exemption concentrate a great deal of power in state authorities without a strong oversight structure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees, which passed it down to their health subcommittees, and it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress adjourned.

narrative.text: Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on June 4, 1991, and it was referred jointly to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees.
Within two weeks it was sent to the Subcommittee on Health in Ways and Means and the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment in Energy and Commerce, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress.
Nine House Democrats signed on as cosponsors, and additional sponsors were added to later printings of the bill text in August 1991 and September 1992, but no committee or floor action followed.
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The health insurance industry and providers kept the existing system untouched, and the roughly 37 million uninsured Americans the bill described gained nothing; no one was ever forced to defend or vote on the proposal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent insurers, providers, and the status quo

for.name: Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Health Care and Cost Containment Act and pursued it through the 102nd Congress.

for.name: 9 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; additional members added their names in later printings of the bill text.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action beyond referring the bill to their health subcommittees in June 1991; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Industry affected by publicly administered state plans
against.what_they_did: Opposed government-run universal health coverage proposals in this era, which would have removed private insurers from covered care in participating states.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split shows in the record; all ten initial sponsors were Sanders and nine Democrats, with no Republican support listed.

industries.note: In any participating state, coverage would be administered by a nonprofit public authority and the state plan would preempt ERISA, removing private insurers from the covered system. Insurers' continued revenue depended on the bill not passing.
They would get guaranteed full payment from the state plan but only through binding global budgets, with extra billing banned — steadier revenue at the cost of a hard spending cap.

Plan payments would be compensation in full with no extra billing allowed, but states could negotiate fees collectively with provider organizations, exempt from antitrust law, and fund scholarships to place doctors in underserved areas.
The state plan's preemption of ERISA would end the employer role as health insurance gatekeeper in participating states, shifting that cost to the public plan funded by taxes.
